analysis.one_liner: Requires binding arbitration when a new union and employer can't agree on a first contract.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote, a floor vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, when workers vote to form a union, the employer must bargain but can drag out talks indefinitely without ever signing a contract. This bill would change that: if no first contract was reached within 60 days of the union vote, the two sides would have to work with a mediator, and if talks still failed after another 30 days, either side could hand the remaining disputes to the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service for binding arbitration. The arbitrator's decision would be final — a contract would exist whether or not the employer agreed to it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at newly unionized workplaces, where employers can legally stall first-contract negotiations for months or years, leaving workers with a union on paper but no raises, benefits, or workplace rules. The bill would guarantee a final, enforceable contract within roughly 90 days of the union election.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who just voted to unionize

how_it_helps.text: If a newly certified union and its employer have no contract within 60 days, the bill requires both sides to work with a mediator on the disputed issues, and lets either side request that the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service pick a mediator if they can't agree on one. [S3]

If mediation hasn't produced a contract within another 30 days, either the employer or the union can send the remaining disputes to the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service for binding arbitration — meaning a final contract is imposed and the stall ends. [S3]
The bill amends the National Labor Relations Act, the federal law governing union organizing and bargaining in the private sector. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing new union organizing lose the ability to let first-contract talks stall indefinitely — a tactic that can leave a union vote toothless. They would have to accept contract terms set by an outside arbitrator if talks fail. Taxpayers bear the modest cost of running the mediation and arbitration process through an existing federal agency.

drawbacks.text: Binding arbitration takes the outcome out of both sides' hands: an arbitrator, not the workers' own negotiators or the employer, would set wages and working conditions, and the resulting contract may fit the workplace less well than one the parties reached themselves. [S3]

A guaranteed endpoint can cut both ways — employers would know a contract is coming no matter what, which some argue reduces their incentive to bargain seriously during the required mediation window. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a well-documented problem: a union election win can mean little when the employer simply never agrees to a first contract. The cost is real but narrow — some contracts would be set by an arbitrator rather than negotiated, and that imposed contract may suit the workplace less well. On balance, workers who just voted for a union get an enforceable agreement they otherwise might never see, at the price of some loss of bargaining control for both sides.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, sent to a subcommittee in February 2005, and never heard from again before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gene Green introduced the bill on January 4, 2005, the opening day of the 109th Congress. [S1] [S5]
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day. [S5]
On February 9, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress. [S5]
No other member signed on as a cosponsor. [S4]
The committee never reported the bill and the House never voted on it; it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who resist newly formed unions keep the ability to stall first-contract negotiations indefinitely, since no version of this fix ever reached a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who stall new union contracts

for.name: Rep. Gene Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; the only sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in January 2005 and never reported it out; the bill went to a subcommittee and no action followed.

against.name: Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after the February 9, 2005 referral and took no action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member besides the Democratic sponsor signed on, so the partisan shape of support and opposition never showed up in the record.

industries.note: The bill would end the practice of letting first-contract talks stall indefinitely after a union election win, forcing employers to accept an arbitrator's contract if they won't agree. That power to stall is what leaves many union votes without real-world effect for workers.
The bill would route new mediation and arbitration cases to this existing federal agency, expanding its role in resolving first-contract disputes.
